etymology: Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield (1851-1921), American Presbyterian theologian. Benjamin (Hebrew, "son of the right hand"); Warfield, an English surname. Known by his initials, "B.B."
biblical_def: Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield (1851-1921) was the last great theologian of "Old Princeton" — the towering Presbyterian scholar who, as professor at Princeton Theological Seminary from 1887 until his death, defended biblical inerrancy and Reformed orthodoxy against the rising tide of theological liberalism and higher criticism. Often called "the Lion of Princeton," Warfield combined immense erudition with polemical force across an extraordinary range: the doctrine of Scripture, Christology, the history of doctrine, apologetics, perfectionism, and the cessation of the miraculous gifts. His essay "The Biblical Idea of Inspiration" and his work with A.A. Hodge on "Inspiration" (1881) gave classic expression to the doctrine of verbal plenary inspiration and inerrancy — that Scripture in its original autographs is the very word of God, without error in all it affirms. His Counterfeit Miracles (1918) is the classic cessationist argument that the miraculous sign-gifts ceased with the apostolic age. He defended the full deity and the two natures of Christ, the Reformed doctrines of grace, and the rationality of Christian faith against both liberal accommodation and irrational fideism. Warfield largely withdrew from public life to care for his invalid wife for decades, pouring his energies into scholarship. His collected works run to ten volumes. He stands as the great defender of confessional Reformed orthodoxy and biblical inerrancy at the moment of liberalism's ascendancy — the bridge between the Old Princeton of Charles Hodge and the fundamentalist-modernist battles that his student J. Gresham Machen would carry forward.
webster_summary: The last great Old Princeton theologian (1851-1921); "the Lion of Princeton"; defender of biblical inerrancy and Reformed orthodoxy against liberalism; author of the classic inerrancy essays and Counterfeit Miracles (the cessationist classic).

corruption_summary: B.B. Warfield is corrupted when his defense of inerrancy is caricatured as wooden literalism, when his Old Princeton apologetic method is dismissed as Enlightenment rationalism, or when his cessationism is forgotten by a charismatic age that has not answered his arguments.
corruption_paragraphs: Wooden-literalism caricature. Warfield's defense of inerrancy is sometimes caricatured as a crude, mechanical literalism that ignores genre, figure, and phenomenon. His actual doctrine is careful: Scripture is without error in all that it affirms, rightly interpreted according to the intent of each passage — including its figures, its phenomenal language, and its literary forms. Warfield distinguished inerrancy (the truth of all Scripture affirms) from a flat literalism that ignores how language works. The caricature attacks a position he did not hold; the doctrine he did hold — that God's word does not err — remains the confessional Reformed position.

Cessationism-forgotten. Warfield's Counterfeit Miracles made the classic case that the miraculous sign-gifts (healing, tongues, prophecy) served to accredit the apostolic foundation and ceased with the apostolic age. The modern charismatic and Pentecostal movements have largely proceeded as though the argument were never made, or as though enthusiasm had answered it. The dictionary's cessationist position (shared with the signs-and-wonders and new-apostolic-reformation entries) stands in Warfield's line: the burden remains on the continuationist to answer the foundational-accreditation argument, not merely to assert present experience.

etymology: Robert Lewis Dabney (1820-1898), American Southern Presbyterian theologian. Robert (Germanic, "bright fame"); Dabney, an English surname of Norman-French origin.
biblical_def: Robert Lewis Dabney (1820-1898) was the leading theologian of 19th-century Southern Presbyterianism — a systematic theologian, churchman, and prolific author whose Systematic Theology (originally Syllabus and Notes, 1871) remains a substantial Reformed text. Dabney taught at Union Theological Seminary in Virginia and later at the University of Texas, and served as chief of staff to Stonewall Jackson during the Civil War, later writing Jackson's biography. As a theologian he was a vigorous defender of confessional Reformed orthodoxy, biblical authority, and the Westminster Standards against the encroachments of theological liberalism, evolutionary thought, and what he saw as the corrosions of modernity. His writing is marked by analytical rigor, polemical sharpness, and a deep commitment to the Reformed system. The dictionary must register an honest difficulty: Dabney was also a defender of the antebellum Southern social order, including slavery, and held views on race that the Scriptures, rightly read, condemn — for all are of one blood (Acts 17:26) and one in Christ (Gal 3:28). This is a real and serious blemish, not to be airbrushed. The Reformed reader honors Dabney's genuine theological contributions — his defense of inerrancy, his systematic rigor, his churchmanship — while plainly rejecting his defense of slavery and his racial views as a failure to follow his own Scriptures to their conclusion. He stands as a sobering example that a man may be theologically acute in many things and gravely wrong in others, and that the dictionary's commitment to truth requires naming both.
webster_summary: Leading Southern Presbyterian theologian (1820-1898); author of a substantial Reformed Systematic Theology; defender of confessional orthodoxy and inerrancy; also a defender of antebellum slavery and racial views Scripture condemns, named here honestly as a serious blemish.

corruption_summary: Robert Dabney is corrupted both when his racial sins are airbrushed by admirers who prize his theology, and when his genuine theological contributions are dismissed wholesale by those who (rightly) condemn his racism; the honest course names both the contribution and the sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Airbrushing the sin. Some admirers of Dabney's theology pass over his defense of slavery and his racial views in embarrassed silence, or minimize them as products of his time. The dictionary refuses this. His defense of the antebellum racial order was a real moral failure, a failure to follow the very Scriptures he defended (Acts 17:26, one blood; Gal 3:28, one in Christ; Jas 2:9, respect of persons is sin) to their plain conclusion. To honor a theologian's orthodoxy is not to excuse his sins; the same Bible Dabney defended condemns the racial hierarchy he upheld. Name the sin plainly.

Dismissing the contribution wholesale. The opposite error, common in the present moment, dismisses everything Dabney wrote because of his racism — as though a man wrong on one grave matter must be wrong on all. This is neither just nor wise. Dabney's defense of biblical inerrancy, his systematic rigor, and his churchmanship retain genuine value, the way Augustine's theology retains value despite his errors, or Luther's despite his late anti-Jewish writings. The mature course holds both truths: a real theological contribution AND a grave moral failure, neither cancelling the other, the contribution received with discernment and the sin named without flinching.

etymology: John Gresham Machen (1881-1937), American Presbyterian theologian. Gresham, an English surname used as his given name; Machen, a Welsh surname. Usually styled "J. Gresham Machen."
biblical_def: John Gresham Machen (1881-1937) was the foremost American defender of confessional Christianity against theological liberalism in the early 20th century — a New Testament scholar, a churchman, and the founder of both Westminster Theological Seminary and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church. Trained at Princeton and in the German universities (where he saw liberalism at its source), Machen taught New Testament at Princeton Seminary under the Old Princeton orthodoxy of Warfield. His most influential book, Christianity and Liberalism (1923), made the decisive argument of the fundamentalist-modernist controversy: that theological liberalism is not a variety of Christianity but a different religion altogether, using Christian vocabulary with non-Christian content (the dictionary's theological-liberalism entry develops this). His scholarly works — The Origin of Paul's Religion (1921) and The Virgin Birth of Christ (1930) — defended the supernatural origin of Christianity against the liberal reconstruction. When Princeton Seminary was reorganized in 1929 to accommodate theological breadth, Machen led the founding of Westminster Theological Seminary (1929) to continue the Old Princeton tradition. When the Presbyterian Church (USA) disciplined him for forming an independent missions board to bypass liberal-controlled denominational missions, he was suspended from the ministry; he responded by leading the formation of the Orthodox Presbyterian Church (1936). He died suddenly in 1937. Machen modeled costly confessional fidelity: he sacrificed his Princeton chair, his denominational standing, and his ministerial credentials rather than make peace with a liberalism he judged to be another religion. His Christianity and Liberalism remains the classic statement of why the difference between historic Christianity and liberalism is not a difference of degree but of kind.

corruption_summary: J. Gresham Machen is corrupted when his fight against liberalism is dismissed as fundamentalist obscurantism, when his scholarship is forgotten behind his polemics, or when the costly separations he led are read as mere divisiveness rather than confessional fidelity.
corruption_paragraphs: Fundamentalist-obscurantist caricature. Machen is sometimes filed under "fundamentalism" and dismissed as an anti-intellectual reactionary. The reality is the reverse: Machen was a Princeton- and German-trained New Testament scholar of the first rank, conversant with the liberalism he opposed at its scholarly source, and respected even by opponents for the quality of his work. He distanced himself from aspects of populist fundamentalism (he disliked the term applied to himself) while defending the supernatural core of Christianity with rigorous scholarship. He fought liberalism not from ignorance but from a deep understanding of exactly what it was.

Divisiveness misreading. Machen led costly separations: from Princeton (founding Westminster), from the PCUSA (founding the OPC). Critics read these as the divisiveness of an uncompromising man. Machen understood them as confessional necessity: when an institution or a denomination has tolerated or embraced another religion under Christian forms, faithfulness may require separation to preserve the gospel itself. He did not separate lightly or first; he separated only after the institutions had themselves abandoned their confessional commitments. The dictionary honors the fidelity that counted the Princeton chair, the denominational standing, and the ministerial credentials as worth losing to keep the faith once delivered (Jude 3).

etymology: Cornelius Van Til (1895-1987), Dutch-American Reformed theologian and apologist. Cornelius (Latin, a Roman gens name; cf. Acts 10); Van Til, a Dutch surname ("from Til").
biblical_def: Cornelius Van Til (1895-1987) was the Dutch-American Reformed theologian who developed presuppositional apologetics — the method of defending the Christian faith that begins from the presupposition of the triune God and the authority of Scripture rather than from supposedly neutral common ground. Born in the Netherlands and raised in a Dutch Reformed immigrant family in America, Van Til was shaped by the Dutch neo-Calvinist tradition of Kuyper and Bavinck. He taught apologetics at Westminster Theological Seminary from its founding (1929) for over forty years. His central conviction was that there is no neutral ground between the believer and the unbeliever: every human being reasons from ultimate commitments, and the unbeliever, while suppressing the truth (Rom 1:18), still depends on the God he denies for the very rationality, logic, and moral order he uses to argue against Him. Van Til therefore rejected the "classical" and "evidentialist" apologetic methods that begin from neutral reason or brute facts and reason up to God; he argued instead that the Christian must challenge the unbeliever's whole worldview, showing that only the Christian worldview, with the self-attesting triune God and His revelation, provides the necessary foundation for reason, science, logic, and ethics — the "transcendental" argument. His thought, dense and demanding, shaped a major stream of Reformed apologetics through students and successors like Greg Bahnsen and John Frame. The dictionary registers that Reformed apologists debate presuppositionalism versus classical method; Van Til's enduring contribution is the insistence that apologetics must be God-centered and Scripture-governed, never conceding a supposedly neutral autonomy to fallen human reason.

corruption_summary: Cornelius Van Til is corrupted when presuppositionalism is caricatured as fideism or circular reasoning, when his rejection of neutral ground is misread as a refusal to give reasons, or when the apologetic-method debate is treated as a test of orthodoxy rather than a genuine intramural Reformed discussion.
corruption_paragraphs: Fideism-and-circularity caricature. Critics charge that presuppositionalism is mere fideism (believe without reasons) or viciously circular (assume God to prove God). Van Til's actual argument is the transcendental one: not "assume God, therefore God," but "the very preconditions of rational thought — logic, the uniformity of nature, moral absolutes — are intelligible only on the Christian worldview, and the unbeliever who uses them is borrowing from the God he denies." This is an argument, not a refusal to argue, and the "circularity" involved is the unavoidable circularity of all ultimate-authority claims (the classicalist's appeal to reason is equally self-referential at the foundation). The caricature mistakes a sophisticated argument for an evasion.

Method-as-orthodoxy-test misreading. The debate between presuppositional and classical/evidentialist apologetics is a genuine intramural discussion among Reformed Christians who share the same confession. Some on each side have treated their method as a test of orthodoxy, dismissing the other as compromised. The dictionary holds that both presuppositionalists (Van Til, Bahnsen, Frame) and classical apologists (the Old Princeton tradition, modern figures like Sproul) are within Reformed orthodoxy, debating method, not the faith itself. Van Til's enduring and widely-shared contribution is the insistence — against any method — that apologetics be God-centered and Scripture-governed, never conceding autonomous neutrality to fallen reason.

etymology: David Martyn Lloyd-Jones (1899-1981), Welsh Reformed preacher. Martyn, a Welsh form of Martin; Lloyd-Jones, a hyphenated Welsh surname. Affectionately known as "the Doctor" for his medical training.
biblical_def: David Martyn Lloyd-Jones (1899-1981) was the Welsh preacher whose expository ministry at Westminster Chapel in London made him the foremost Reformed pulpit voice of 20th-century Britain and a key figure in the recovery of Reformed, experiential, Puritan-influenced preaching in the English-speaking world. Trained as a physician (hence his lifelong nickname "the Doctor"), Lloyd-Jones abandoned a promising medical career under a sense of gospel calling and entered the ministry, first in his native Wales and then, from 1938 to 1968, at Westminster Chapel. His preaching was marked by careful, sustained biblical exposition, a deep concern for the experiential reality of the Spirit's work, and a powerful sense of the "unction" or anointing of the Spirit upon preaching. His great sermon series — on Romans (fourteen volumes), Ephesians, the Sermon on the Mount, and Spiritual Depression — were transcribed and published, shaping pastors worldwide. He championed the recovery of the Puritans (his addresses founded the Puritan Conference and inspired the Banner of Truth Trust), called evangelicals to doctrinal seriousness, and pressed the necessity of the new birth and the experiential knowledge of God against a merely intellectual or nominal Christianity. His Preaching and Preachers (1971) remains a classic on the preacher's task. The dictionary notes one area of ongoing discussion: Lloyd-Jones held a view of the "baptism with the Spirit" as a distinct, often post-conversion experience of assurance and power, which cessationists and some Reformed have questioned; this did not make him a charismatic in the modern sense, but it distinguished his pneumatology from strict cessationism. His enduring legacy is the recovery of weighty, doctrinal, experiential, expository preaching.

corruption_summary: Martyn Lloyd-Jones is corrupted when his emphasis on the Spirit's unction is mistaken for charismatic enthusiasm, when his expository legacy is reduced to technique, or when his call to experiential religion is confused with the modern therapeutic or mystical alternatives he opposed.
corruption_paragraphs: Charismatic-enthusiasm confusion. Lloyd-Jones's emphasis on the Spirit's power upon preaching, and his particular view of the baptism with the Spirit as an experience of assurance and power, have led some to claim him for the charismatic movement and others to suspect him of it. Neither is accurate. Lloyd-Jones was a confessional Calvinist who prized doctrine, expository preaching, and the Puritans; his concern for the experiential power of the Spirit was a concern that sound doctrine be accompanied by real spiritual life and unction, not a turn toward tongues, prophecy, or the sign-gifts. His pneumatology differed from strict cessationism, but his ministry was the opposite of charismatic enthusiasm: weighty, doctrinal, and Word-centered.

Experiential-as-therapeutic confusion. Lloyd-Jones called relentlessly for experiential religion — the real, felt, transforming knowledge of God, the necessity of the new birth, the difference between knowing about God and knowing God. In a therapeutic age this can be misheard as a call to religious feeling for its own sake, or to self-fulfillment. His Spiritual Depression is the antidote to the misreading: he diagnoses the believer's discouragement not by validating feelings but by preaching truth to the soul ("you have to take yourself in hand, address yourself, preach to yourself"). His experiential religion was the application of hard doctrine to the heart, the opposite of the therapeutic self-focus that came after him.

etymology: James Innell Packer (1926-2020), English-Canadian Reformed Anglican theologian. James (from Hebrew Jacob); Packer, an English occupational surname. Usually styled "J.I. Packer."
biblical_def: James Innell Packer (1926-2020) was the English-Canadian Reformed Anglican theologian whose Knowing God (1973) became one of the most beloved and widely-read works of 20th-century evangelical theology, and who labored across a long life to recover the Puritans and Reformed experiential religion for the modern church. Educated at Oxford, Packer was shaped by his discovery of the Puritans (especially John Owen on indwelling sin and the mortification of sin) and became a leading voice for Reformed, experiential, doctrinally-serious evangelicalism. His 1958 introduction to a reprint of Owen's Death of Death in the Death of Christ is a landmark essay recovering definite atonement for modern readers (the dictionary's definite-atonement entry notes it). Knowing God (1973), his most famous book, presents the doctrine of God not as cold abstraction but as the ground of a transforming personal knowledge of God — doctrine for the sake of communion. His Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God (1961) showed that divine sovereignty and human responsibility are not at odds in evangelism but are an "antinomy" the believer holds together without resolving away either truth. Packer taught for many years at Regent College in Vancouver and served as general editor of the English Standard Version. The dictionary registers points of discussion: Packer's signing of "Evangelicals and Catholics Together" (1994) drew sharp Reformed criticism for appearing to blur the gospel distinctives the Reformation recovered, and some questioned his later ecumenical engagements. These genuine concerns notwithstanding, Packer's enduring gift was to make weighty Reformed theology accessible and devotional — doctrine that leads to the knowledge of God and the worship of Him.
webster_summary: English-Canadian Reformed Anglican theologian (1926-2020); author of Knowing God (1973); recovered the Puritans (esp. Owen) and definite atonement for modern readers; ESV general editor; doctrine for the sake of communion with God.

corruption_summary: J.I. Packer is corrupted when Knowing God is read as devotional comfort detached from its hard doctrine, when his ecumenical engagements are either ignored or used to dismiss his whole contribution, or when his recovery of the Puritans is forgotten behind his popular fame.
corruption_paragraphs: Devotional-detached-from-doctrine misreading. Knowing God is beloved as a warm devotional book, and some read it for comfort while skating over its theological backbone. Packer's whole point was that the warmth comes FROM the doctrine: one knows God truly only by knowing the truth about God — His sovereignty, holiness, wrath, grace, and majesty. The book is an exposition of the doctrine of God aimed at communion, not a substitute for doctrine. To read it as gentle inspiration detached from its hard theology is to miss Packer's thesis that there is no real knowing of God apart from sound doctrine of God.

ECT and the gospel distinctives. Packer's signing of "Evangelicals and Catholics Together" (1994) drew sharp and substantive criticism from Reformed leaders (including R.C. Sproul and others) who judged that the document blurred the very gospel distinctives — justification by faith alone — that the Reformation had recovered against Rome. The dictionary takes this concern seriously: the criticism was not pettiness but a defense of sola fide. At the same time, it would be unjust to let one contested document erase a lifetime of genuine service to Reformed truth. The mature course names the real concern about ECT plainly while continuing to receive, with discernment, Packer's enduring gifts to the church — Knowing God, the recovery of Owen, the defense of definite atonement, and his lifelong call to doctrine-for-communion.

etymology: Robert Charles Sproul (1939-2017), American Reformed theologian. Robert (Germanic, "bright fame"); Sproul, a Scottish surname. Usually styled "R.C. Sproul."
biblical_def: Robert Charles Sproul (1939-2017) was the American Reformed theologian, teacher, and broadcaster whose gift for clear, compelling instruction made him one of the most influential popularizers of Reformed theology in the late 20th and early 21st centuries. Sproul founded Ligonier Ministries (1971), an immense teaching ministry whose conferences, broadcasts (the daily Renewing Your Mind program), and publications brought Reformed doctrine to a vast audience. His most famous book, The Holiness of God (1985), recovered for a generation the biblical vision of God's transcendent holiness and the creature's proper trembling before it, built around Isaiah's vision in the temple (Isa 6). He defended biblical inerrancy as a principal framer of the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978), classical apologetics, justification by faith alone (he was a leading critic of "Evangelicals and Catholics Together" precisely to defend sola fide), and the doctrines of grace (his Chosen by God made the Reformed doctrine of election accessible to ordinary readers). Sproul also founded Reformation Bible College and pastored Saint Andrew's Chapel in Florida. His teaching combined doctrinal precision with a rare clarity and an evident delight in the truth; he could make the hardest doctrines — election, the holiness of God, the atonement — both intelligible and weighty for the layman. Through Ligonier he equipped a generation of believers in confessional Reformed theology. The dictionary honors Sproul as the great modern teacher who made Reformed doctrine clear without making it shallow, and who defended the gospel distinctives of the Reformation in his own day.

corruption_summary: R.C. Sproul is corrupted when his gift for clarity is mistaken for shallowness, when his popularizing role is set against scholarship as though accessible doctrine were lesser doctrine, or when his defenses of inerrancy and sola fide are forgotten behind his fame as a broadcaster.
corruption_paragraphs: Clarity-as-shallowness misreading. Sproul made the hardest doctrines accessible to ordinary believers — election, the holiness of God, the atonement, inerrancy. Some mistake accessibility for shallowness, as though doctrine made clear must be doctrine made thin. The reverse is true: it takes deep mastery to teach a hard thing clearly, and Sproul's clarity rested on genuine theological depth and precision. He did not dumb down the doctrines; he opened them. The gift of making the weighty intelligible to the layman is a high and rare gift, not a lesser one.

Popularizer-versus-scholar misreading. Because Sproul's primary calling was teaching the church rather than producing academic monographs, he is sometimes filed as a mere popularizer, beneath the serious theologians. This misjudges both the man and the calling. Sproul was a careful theologian who chose to spend his gifts equipping the ordinary believer — a calling the church desperately needs and too often despises. Through Ligonier he did more to ground a generation in confessional Reformed theology than many a scholar reaching only the academy. The dictionary honors the teacher of the church as highly as the teacher of the academy.

etymology: James Montgomery Boice (1938-2000), American Reformed pastor and theologian. James (from Hebrew Jacob); Boice, an American surname. Usually styled "James Montgomery Boice."
biblical_def: James Montgomery Boice (1938-2000) was the American Reformed pastor, expositor, and broadcaster who pastored Tenth Presbyterian Church in Philadelphia for over thirty years and labored, through preaching, radio, and writing, for the recovery of Reformed, expository, gospel-centered ministry in late-20th-century evangelicalism. Educated at Harvard and at the University of Basel (where he studied under the shadow of European theology), Boice returned to pastor Tenth Presbyterian, one of the historic pulpits of American Presbyterianism, from 1968 until his death in 2000. His expository ministry produced massive commentary series — on Genesis, the Psalms, the Gospel of John, Romans, and the Minor Prophets — transcribed from his preaching. He was the longtime speaker on The Bible Study Hour radio broadcast and a founder and chairman of the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy, which produced the Chicago Statement (1978). Late in his life, alarmed by the drift of evangelicalism toward pragmatism, man-centered worship, and a diluted gospel, Boice helped found the Alliance of Confessing Evangelicals and was a principal author of the Cambridge Declaration (1996), which recalled the church to the five solas of the Reformation against the encroachments of the modern church-growth and seeker-sensitive movements. Diagnosed with aggressive cancer, Boice preached to his congregation about the sovereignty of God in his dying with a faith that moved many; he died weeks later, having written a final hymn. He stands as a model of the Reformed pastor-theologian: a faithful expositor of one pulpit for a generation, a defender of inerrancy and the solas, and a man whose dying magnified the God he had preached.

corruption_summary: James Montgomery Boice is corrupted when his decades of faithful expository ministry are forgotten behind flashier names, when the Cambridge Declaration's call to the solas is treated as mere nostalgia, or when his model of the settled pastor-theologian is despised in an age of celebrity and platform.
corruption_paragraphs: Settled-pastorate undervalued. Boice pastored one church for thirty-two years — the unglamorous, faithful, long obedience of expository ministry in a single pulpit. In an age that prizes platform, mobility, and the building of personal brands, the model of the settled pastor-theologian who pours his life into one congregation can seem small. It is not. Boice's massive commentary series, his radio ministry, and his confessional leadership all flowed from the faithful weekly exposition of Scripture to one people over decades. The dictionary honors the long obedience of the settled pulpit as the model it is.

Cambridge-Declaration-as-nostalgia misreading. The Cambridge Declaration (1996), which Boice helped author through the Alliance of Confessing Evangelicals, recalled evangelicalism to the five solas of the Reformation against the man-centered, pragmatic, market-driven church of the church-growth movement. Some hear this as backward-looking nostalgia for a Reformation long past. The dictionary hears it as a prophetic call: the solas — Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone, Christ alone, to God's glory alone — are not period pieces but the permanent shape of the gospel, and Boice's generation needed the recall as much as Luther's needed the original. The drift the Declaration named (the church-growth-movement and seeker-sensitive entries develop it) has only deepened; the recall is more, not less, urgent.

etymology: Sinclair Buchanan Ferguson (b. 1948), Scottish Reformed theologian and pastor. Sinclair, a Scottish surname used as a given name; Ferguson, a Scottish surname.
biblical_def: Sinclair Buchanan Ferguson (born 1948) is a Scottish Reformed theologian, pastor, and author widely esteemed for combining rigorous theological scholarship with warm pastoral and experiential application in the best Scottish-Puritan tradition. Ferguson has pastored in Scotland and in the United States (including First Presbyterian Church, Columbia, South Carolina) and has taught systematic theology at Westminster Theological Seminary and elsewhere. His scholarly work includes a major study of John Owen and a respected volume on the Holy Spirit in the Contours of Christian Theology series. His most influential popular-level book, The Whole Christ (2016), revisits the Marrow Controversy (the dictionary's marrow-controversy entry) to address the perennial dangers of legalism and antinomianism, arguing that both spring from the same root — a failure to grasp the free grace of the gospel and the gift of Christ Himself — and that the remedy for both is not a middle path between them but the whole Christ offered freely in the gospel. Ferguson is a teaching fellow with Ligonier Ministries and a frequent conference speaker, known for the unusual combination of doctrinal depth, historical learning, pastoral tenderness, and Scottish wit. He stands in the living line of Reformed, experiential, Christ-centered theology — a contemporary heir of the Puritans and the Marrow Men, laboring to keep the gospel of free grace clear against the recurring distortions of legalism and license.

corruption_summary: Sinclair Ferguson is corrupted when The Whole Christ's diagnosis is reduced to a slogan, when his pastoral warmth is severed from his doctrinal rigor, or when the legalism-antinomianism analysis is misheard as advocating a soft middle path rather than the free grace of the whole Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Middle-path misreading. Ferguson's The Whole Christ argues that legalism and antinomianism are not opposite ends of a spectrum with the truth in the middle, but twin errors springing from the same root — a failure to grasp the free grace of the gospel, a suspicion that God is not truly generous, that drives one soul toward law-keeping for acceptance and another toward license against restraint. The remedy is not a moderate balance between legalism and antinomianism but the whole Christ Himself, freely given, in whom both the demand for righteousness and the freedom from condemnation are met. To read Ferguson as commending a cautious middle path is to miss his actual thesis: the gospel of free grace dissolves both errors at their common root.

Warmth-severed-from-rigor misreading. Ferguson is beloved for pastoral warmth and gentleness, and some receive him as a comforting teacher while bypassing the theological rigor beneath. His warmth rests on serious scholarship — a major study of Owen, careful work on pneumatology, deep engagement with the Marrow tradition. Like the best of the Scottish-Puritan line he embodies, his tenderness is the fruit of doctrine, not a substitute for it. The pastoral application flows from the theological depth; sever them and you lose both the depth that gives the warmth its substance and the warmth that gives the depth its purpose.

etymology: Joel Robert Beeke (b. 1952), American Reformed theologian, pastor, and educator of Dutch Reformed heritage. Joel (Hebrew, "Yahweh is God"); Beeke, a Dutch surname.
biblical_def: Joel Robert Beeke (born 1952) is an American Reformed theologian, pastor, and educator of the Dutch Reformed experiential tradition who has labored prolifically for the recovery of Puritan and Dutch Further Reformation (Nadere Reformatie) experiential piety in the modern church. A minister in the Heritage Reformed Congregations, Beeke is the founder and longtime president of Puritan Reformed Theological Seminary in Grand Rapids, Michigan, and the founder of Reformation Heritage Books, a major publisher of Reformed and Puritan literature. He has authored, co-authored, or edited an extraordinary number of works — including A Puritan Theology: Doctrine for Life (with Mark Jones), a massive systematic survey of Puritan doctrine, and Reformed Systematic Theology (a multi-volume work) — and has overseen the publication of countless Puritan and Reformed reprints. His central emphasis is "experiential" or "experimental" Reformed Christianity: the conviction that sound doctrine must be experienced in the heart and lived in practice, in the tradition of the Puritans and the Dutch Further Reformation divines (Voetius, à Brakel, and others) for whom theology was always "doctrine for life." Beeke combines confessional precision (he holds firmly to the Three Forms of Unity and esteems the Westminster Standards) with a pastoral concern for the marks of grace in the soul, assurance of salvation, and the cultivation of godliness. He stands as a contemporary bridge between the English Puritan and the Dutch Reformed experiential traditions, and as one of the most industrious laborers for the recovery of that heritage in the present-day Reformed world.

corruption_summary: Joel Beeke is corrupted when experiential Reformed Christianity is mistaken for subjective mysticism, when the marks-of-grace emphasis tips toward morbid introspection, or when his prolific output is dismissed as quantity over quality rather than as labor for the church's recovery of its heritage.
corruption_paragraphs: Experiential-as-mysticism misreading. Beeke's emphasis on "experiential" or "experimental" religion — the heart-experience of doctrine, the felt knowledge of God, the marks of grace in the soul — can be misheard as a turn toward subjective mysticism or emotionalism. The Reformed experiential tradition Beeke represents is the opposite: it is the application of objective doctrine to the soul, the insistence that the truths of God's Word be not merely known but experienced and lived. "Experimental" in the older sense means "tested by experience" — doctrine proven in the crucible of the Christian life. It is doctrine-for-life, anchored in the objective Word, not feeling unmoored from truth.

Introspection-tipping concern. The experiential tradition's attention to the marks of grace and the assurance of salvation carries a real pastoral danger, which Beeke himself is aware of: that the believer turns endlessly inward, searching his own heart for sufficient evidence of grace, and falls into morbid introspection and the loss of assurance. The healthy form of the tradition (and Beeke's own counsel) directs the troubled soul finally outward and upward — to Christ Himself and the promises of the gospel — not merely inward to the inventory of his own graces. The marks of grace confirm; they do not found. Assurance rests ultimately on Christ and His promise, examined-but-not-replaced by the evidence of grace within. The dictionary commends the experiential tradition while noting the introspective danger it must guard against.
